title_en: Hong Kong Election Committee race: turnout reaches 96% in mid-afternoon voting
content_en:
WKCDA head Bernard Chan says geopolitics and tech shifts are top challenges for Hong Kong’s next leader as 3pm polling draws 5,458 voters.
Harbour Road Sports Centre polling station in Wan Chai. First-hour polling has drawn a 45 per cent turnout. Photo: Karma Lo
Voting has been under way for more than seven hours at five polling stations across Hong Kong on Sunday, with about two hours left to select members of the powerful Election Committee, which is tasked with choosing the city’s next leader.
A total of 856 candidates are vying for 723 seats across the 31 subsectors. The elected members will join 259 members from five uncontested subsectors, 362 ex officio members and 156 members nominated by designated bodies to form the 1,500-strong electoral college.
The key body will nominate and vote in next year’s chief executive election, and will nominate candidates and elect 40 of the 90 lawmakers in the 2029 Legislative Council election.
The second Election Committee poll since Beijing’s electoral overhaul in 2021 to ensure only patriots hold power is set to be more competitive than the ballot five years ago, when only 13 subsectors held contested races.
Excluding uncontested subsectors, only 5,709 voters are eligible to cast ballots on Sunday, including government-appointed district representatives, corporate bodies named by authorities and government-subsidised NGOs.
With ramped-up mobilisation and campaigning in the final stage, Beijing expects turnout to surpass 89.77 per cent in 2021 and reach at least 90 per cent.
The South China Morning Post speaks to voters on the ground and tracks the turnout as ballots are cast. The full list of candidates can be seen here.
Reporting by Matthew Cheng, Lam Ka-sing and Leopold Chen.
Supporters gather at Harbour Road Sports Centre polling station in Wan Chai. Photo: Karma Lo
Property tycoon, medical leader cast ballots
Footfall remains light at the Wan Chai polling station into the afternoon.
Among those entering the polling station at around 3pm are Cheng Chi-man, president of the Hong Kong Medical Association, and Vincent Lo Hong-sui, chairman of Shui On Group.
Neither respond to questions from the press.
As of 3pm, the overall turnout reached 95.6 per cent, with 5,458 voters casting their ballots.
Afternoon voters cite ‘civic duty’
An elderly voter surnamed Ho in the social welfare sector says he visited the Kowloon Park Sports Centre voting station to “fulfil civic duty”.
“Citizens should do this,” Ho says. “It is important because it concerns Hongkongers’ welfare.”
He notes the station was “quiet” with few people around 2.30pm.
“It is very smooth. It is done well,” Ho says.
The social welfare sector has a cumulative turnout of 71.78 per cent as of 2pm.
Another middle-aged voter in the industrial (second) sector who declines to give his name says he turned up out of civic duty.
He notes most people had voted already while holding in his hands a government letter that he takes to the station.
The industrial (second) sector has a cumulative turnout of 91.09 per cent as of 2pm.
Turnout reaches nearly 94 per cent at 2pm
As of 2pm, overall turnout has reached 93.55 per cent, with 5,341 of the 5,709 registered electors having voted.
Across the 31 contested subsectors, five have seen a turnout rate of 100 per cent, including commercial (third), industrial (first), accountancy, legal, and technology and innovation.
The finance subsector records the lowest turnout rate so far, standing at 69.12 per cent.
Legislative Council President Starry Lee Wai-king visits a polling station in Wan Chai, describing the election as historic and saying it will select representative and competent Election Committee members.
“Many voters have already arrived since this morning. I urge all voters once again to come out and cast their ballots actively. I am very confident about the turnout,” Lee says.
Tam Yiu-chung, a former Hong Kong deputy to the National People’s Congress Standing Committee, the country’s top legislative body, also says fiercer competition is driving up turnout, calling it a main factor behind the record voter participation.
He earlier told the SCMP that he expects turnout to surpass 90 per cent, but that achieving 100 per cent would be challenging.
Daughter of gambling tycoon casts ballot
Businesswoman Pansy Ho Chiu-king, daughter of late Macau gambling tycoon Stanley Ho Hung-sun, has cast her ballot at Wan Chai polling station at around 2.15pm.
Ho, an executive chairwoman and managing director of Shun Tak Holdings, has been an ex officio member of the Election Committee.
Ho stayed for around 10 minutes and did not respond to reporters’ questions including whether she supports the re-election of Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu.
Pansy Ho (centre) at Wan Chai polling station. Photo: Karma Lo
Campaigners and voters take lunch break
With most campaigning crowds outside the station gone, the area has become quieter around lunchtime, with only a handful of voters coming to cast their ballots.
Kelvin Wong, a voter in his sixties in the wholesale and retail sector, says the Kowloon Park Sports Centre voting centre has fewer voters at around 1.50pm.
“There are only three or five people,” Wong says.
He notes there were fewer people in the last election too.
Another voter in the import and export sector, who declined to give his name, says he came in the afternoon after attending to some personal matters in the morning.
“I came early at 8 to 9am last time,” he says.
He notes that the most people voted around 8am and 9am and voting count already reached over 80 per cent by 1pm, leaving fewer people at the station.
Geopolitics, tech advancement remain top challenges: Bernard Chan
Bernard Chan, chairman of Asia Financial Holdings and Asia Insurance and head of the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority board, casts his ballot at the Wan Chai polling station.
He says geopolitical tensions and technological advancements remain the greatest challenges for the next city leader and other public officeholders, placing them under intense pressure.
“I believe anyone taking up public office in the future will face major challenges they may never have encountered before,” Chan says.
He notes that the current government has helped Hong Kong get back on track after the chaos following the 2019 social unrest while tackling numerous difficulties.
“However, these challenges will keep coming; they are not short-term challenges, including geopolitics and new technologies that upend our economic model,” Chan adds.
“I hope that all elected Election Committee members can make the right choices regarding Hong Kong’s future development and that of the country.”
Voter turnout surpasses 2021 total
As of 1pm, turnout for the Election Committee poll stands at 89.81 per cent – already surpassing the 89.77 per cent overall turnout recorded in 2021.
So far, 5,127 of the 5,709 eligible electors have cast their ballots.
Across the 31 contested subsectors, commercial (third) and technology and innovation see a 100 per cent turnout, the highest among all subsectors.
Another 10 subsectors see turnout rates above 90 per cent, including commercial (first), wholesale and retail, and legal and grass roots associations.
Social welfare remains the subsector with the lowest turnout, standing at 60.74 per cent.
Vote count to be completed within ‘reasonable time frame’
While the 2021 poll took more than 14 hours to count votes because of glitches in the counting machines, Electoral Affairs Commission chairman David Lok Kai-hong says authorities reviewed the process after the previous election and improved the electronic counting systems, which ran smoothly and efficiently in last year’s by-election.
“The Electoral Affairs Commission generally does not predict how long vote counting will take. From our perspective, the most important thing is that the election is fair and impartial,” Lok says.
“But I think I can say here that we are confident the vote counting this time can be completed within a reasonable time frame.”
Electoral Affairs Commission chairman David Lok (second right) says vote counting can be completed “within a reasonable time frame”. Photo: Karma Lo
Lok is also satisfied with this morning’s voting procedures, saying polling stations are running smoothly and electors are casting their ballots in an orderly manner with sufficient voting booths, despite large numbers of voters flocking to the polls.
“The Electoral Affairs Commission does not comment on the turnout rate, nor do we set any target for voter turnout,” Lok adds.
“We certainly hope to encourage and appeal to all eligible voters to please come out and cast their ballots today.”
Speaking to the media after inspecting a polling station in Wan Chai, Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak Mei-kuen says the election atmosphere is enthusiastic and orderly.
“Every candidate and their campaign team wants to build recognition and win support from voters. Everyone can see that things have been very orderly,” Mak says.
“It reflects Hong Kong’s democratic development; everyone is making progress towards high-quality democracy.”
‘John Lee is very competent’
Chan Wing-kee, a former standing committee member of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference and a candidate in the industrial (second) subsector, praises city leader Lee’s performance.
“Let’s see how things develop. I am very satisfied with the incumbent chief executive,” Chan says.
“I think the current chief executive is very competent, and I am also quite satisfied with how he has handled various matters.”
However, he stops short of saying whether he will support Lee for a second term.
“Hong Kong has many capable people, so whoever becomes the next chief executive, I will vote for the one with the strongest ability,” Chan adds.
“If I become an Election Committee member, I will choose the most capable candidate, although that doesn’t mean their opponent isn’t good.”
When asked whether he expects a contest in the next city leader race, he says the situation remains unclear. “We’ll just see how things unfold,” he adds
Meanwhile, Wingco Lo Kam-wing, president of the Chinese Manufacturers’ Association of Hong Kong, says he expects elected members to lead the industrial sector’s upgrading and transformation.
As an ex officio member, he also calls on the next city leader to implement Hong Kong’s first five-year plan well.
“Hong Kong’s economy must transform. Alongside our traditional industries, we need to cultivate more emerging sectors while building [the city] into an international innovation and technology centre,” Lo says.
“That will take an all-of-society effort, with both the government and the business community working together to foster Hong Kong’s future economic development.”
More tycoons have also been seen casting their ballots at the polling station in Wan Chai, including Henry Cheng Kar-shun, chairman of New World Development, and Douglas Woo Chun-kuen, chairman of Wheelock and Company Limited.
Highly competitive race: Regina Ip
Regina Ip Lau Suk-yee, chairwoman of the New People’s Party, canvasses for her party’s candidates outside the polling station in Wan Chai. She describes the race as “highly competitive”, noting the vibrant atmosphere and long queues at the polling station.
“We are a small party. We have a limited number of candidates in the commerce subsectors, mostly in the district committees subsectors,” Ip says. “We are aiming for a 90 per cent success rate.”
She declines to comment on next year’s chief executive election.
Convenor of the Executive Council Regina Ip (second left) at the Harbour Road Sports Centre polling station in Wan Chai. Photo: Karma Lo
Meanwhile, Lo Wai-kwok, chairman of the Business and Professionals Alliance for Hong Kong, expresses confidence that elected Election Committee members will choose the next chief executive wisely, and calls on eligible electors to cast their ballots.
“Competition in this election is intense. Each subsector draws top talent across generations, including newcomers and veterans,” Lo says. “This merit-based selection process will produce Election Committee members we can truly rely on.”
However, Lo declines to comment on the next city leader, stressing only that the person should go all out to improve Hong Kong’s economy and people’s livelihoods.
“In our exchanges [with voters], we’ve had in-depth discussions on advancing Hong Kong’s economy and people’s livelihoods – especially the Northern Metropolis – and on how to align with national needs while playing to Hong Kong’s strengths,” he adds.
Turnout rate surpasses 80 per cent
A total of 4,740 voters have cast their ballots as of 12pm, representing an overall turnout of 83.03 per cent, significantly higher than the 45.92 per cent recorded during the same period in 2021.
Across the 31 contested subsectors, commercial (third), which represents the Hong Kong Chinese Enterprises Association, recorded a turnout of 100 per cent, the highest among all subsectors. All 113 voters of the subsector have voted.
The turnout of eight other subsectors has also surpassed 90 per cent, including commercial (first); industrial (first); legal; technology and innovation; agriculture and fisheries; grass roots associations; representatives of members of area committees, district fight crime committees and district fire safety committees of Hong Kong and Kowloon, and representatives of members of area committees, district fight crime committees and district fire safety committees of the New Territories.
The social welfare subsector has recorded the lowest turnout so far at 53.37 per cent.
Secretary for Constitutional and Mainland Affairs Janice Tse Siu-wa was seen inspecting the polling station in Wan Chai before noon.
‘Good atmosphere proves election’s value’
Lau Wing-keung, an elderly voter in the Heung Yee Kuk sector, visits the Kowloon Park Sports Centre polling station before 11am, noting that time slot is better to avoid the crowds.
He notes there are more people than the last election.
“It is much more convenient when they congregate the voting stations to a few places, that is less scattered,” Lau says.
“Canvassing for votes is a sort of support for the election. It has a good atmosphere, which proves the election is useful in electing the chief executive.”
Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak Mei-kuen visits the station in the morning and leaves at around 11.20am with her staff.
First hour sees record turnout of 45 per cent
Among the 5,709 registered voters, 2,554 cast their ballots in the first hour of polling, representing an overall turnout of 44.74 per cent, more than triple the 14.73 per cent recorded during the same period in 2021.
Across the 31 contested subsectors, commercial (third), which represents the Hong Kong Chinese Enterprises Association, records a turnout of 98.23 per cent, the highest among all subsectors.
The turnout in five other subsectors has also surpassed 50 per cent, including legal; industrial (first); agriculture and fisheries; grass roots associations; and representatives of members of area committees, district fight crime committees and district fire safety committees of Hong Kong and Kowloon.
By contrast, commercial (second), representing the Chinese General Chamber of Commerce, has recorded the lowest turnout so far at 16.16 per cent, with just 16 of its 99 registered voters having cast their ballots.
In the first hour of the 2021 election, the labour subsector recorded the highest turnout at 29.73 per cent, while education had the lowest at 7.49 per cent. Both subsectors are uncontested this year.
Kowloon Park Sports Centre polling station in Tsim Sha Tsui on Sunday. Photo: Karma Lo
Technology used for canvassing support, verification
Vincent Kwok, a technology sector voter in his early fifties, says he arrived at the Kowloon Park Sports Centre polling station at about 9.35am.
He notes that there is more enthusiastic canvassing by candidates and voters this time than last election.
“I feel the atmosphere is very good,” Kwok says. “Everyone wants to contribute to this.”
Despite waiting in line to vote, he says the arrangements are well organised.
“I had to wait in there. It seems it is more enthusiastic this year,” he says. “By my observation, I waited more than 10 minutes. There were around 70 to 80 people for my line.”
Kwok says voters were seated while waiting and the process was smooth.
“I thought we could go straight in but we had to sit,” Kwok says. “But it’s OK. It’s quite smooth.”
He says all candidates explained their platforms and directions to voters like him via WhatsApp, WeChat, email and online conference clearly.
He highlights the use of technology at the station, noting voters’ identities were double-checked and ballots were scanned for verification to ensure everyone voted successfully.
Over 100 voters line up before voting starts
Hundreds of campaigners canvass support by raising placards with candidates’ names, numbers and categories along Austin Road outside the polling station at Kowloon Park Sports Centre.
Voters gradually show up, walking to the station early Sunday morning.
Raymond Chui, 59, a voter for Representatives of members of Area Committees, District Fight Crime Committees, and District Fire Safety Committees of the New Territories, says he has come early to vote before going to work to support the election.
He says competition appears keener than the last election.
“I came around 8.45am. More than 100 people had already lined up there,” says Chui. “I was more than 150th in line.”
He notes that candidates are more enthusiastic in canvassing for support than last time.
“They were very enthusiastic, filling the road up to the taxi stop of B P International hotel,” Chui says.
Apart from taking to the streets, candidates tried to reach voters like him via WhatsApp, WeChat and physical mail, Chui adds.
Waiting times up to 30 minutes for voters in Wan Chai
As most voters head to the polls in the morning, some electors say they have been waiting nearly half an hour to cast their ballots at the Harbour Road Sports Centre polling station.
An insurance subsector voter, who asks to be identified only by his surname, Fung, says he sees more than 100 people queuing inside the venue and that it took him nearly 40 minutes to vote, though he stresses the overall process is smooth.
Lawmaker Jonathan Leung Chun, who is voting in the catering subsector, says he queued for 20 minutes, adding that instructions inside are clear despite the lengthy wait.
However, some electors have opted to leave and return later in the day because of the long lines. One voter who declines to give her name notes that more than 100 constituents were waiting and says she will come back later.
Voters wait in a seating area at Harbour Road Sport Centre polling station. Photo: Karma Lo
Outside the polling station, hundreds of campaign workers line both sides of the pedestrian walkways, chanting slogans and making final-stretch appeals for support.
Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung arrives at the polling station at around 9.15am to inspect security arrangements. More than a dozen police officers are deployed nearby, while Civil Aid Service personnel repeatedly urge campaign teams to keep the pathways clear for incoming voters.
Several prominent business figures have also turned up to vote, including Pacific Century Group chairman Richard Li Tzar-kai. He declines to speak to the media when asked about his expectations for the incoming Election Committee. Hopewell Holdings founder Gordon Wu Ying-sheung is also seen at the polling station.
Allan Zeman backs city leader Lee for another term
Voters have flocked to cast their ballots at the Harbour Road Sports Centre polling station.
Lan Kwai Fong Group chairman Allan Zeman, who is both a voter and a candidate seeking re-election in the catering subsector, voices support for Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu to run for a second term as the city’s leader.
“If he’s one of the candidates running, I will support [him for re-election],” Zeman says, praising Lee as an approachable leader with a results-oriented approach to governance.
“He has done a very good job. And speaking to other businesspeople, they all agree he’s one of the best we’ve had.”
Zeman also says he expects incoming Election Committee members to have a strong grasp of Hong Kong’s needs and help the city navigate geopolitical tensions.
Meanwhile, Tai Po district councillor Armstrong Lee Hon-cheung, a voter in the district representatives subsector, says he is weighing candidates based on their community service record.
“I mainly look at their past track record and commitment to district service, as well as whether they have substantive, concrete proposals for Hong Kong’s future,” Lee says.
“I hope to find someone with long-term vision and a sense of responsibility towards Hong Kong, who will genuinely carry out practical work on people’s livelihoods to help all sectors of society – especially the grass roots and the sandwich class.”
Polling stations open at 9am
Voters have filed into polling stations as they opened at 9am. The five voting stations are located in Harbour Road Sports Centre in Wan Chai, Kowloon Park Sports Centre in Tsim Sha Tsui, Tsuen Wan Sports Centre in Tsuen Wan, Tiu Keng Leng Sports Centre in Tseung Kwan O, and Che Kung Temple Sports Centre in Sha Tin.
Two dedicated polling stations have also been set up at Happy Valley Police Station and Shek Pik Prison for electors in custody.
The polling hours run from 9am to 6pm. After the poll closes, ballot papers will be transported to the counting station at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai for vote counting.
Harbour Road Sports Centre polling station. A total of 856 candidates are vying for 723 seats across the 31 subsectors. Photo: Karma Lo
Final push to boost voter turnout
In the run-up to the election, the government, political parties and community groups have stepped up mobilisation to urge electors to cast their ballots. Candidates have also ramped up street-level campaigning, with magnates and former senior officials taking to the streets to hand out leaflets.
Lau Siu-kai, a consultant to the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said Beijing hoped Election Committee members would bridge the gap with the general public through street-level campaigning and better represent their interests when selecting the city leader and lawmakers.
Tam Yiu-chung, a former Hong Kong member of the National People’s Congress Standing Committee, mainland China’s top legislative body, said earlier that the more competitive election would drive up voter turnout.
He anticipated the turnout rate would reach 90 per cent after more thorough mobilisation than the 2021 poll, a figure he described as one Beijing “will be pleased to see”.
Veteran political commentator Sonny Lo Shiu-hing also said that the turnout rate would signal the effectiveness of Beijing’s mobilisation in the final stretch, adding that higher voter participation would give the elected members greater legitimacy.
Heavyweights joining the race
Dozens of high-profile candidates, including former senior officials and tycoons, also stand in the race.
Prominent newcomers include former justice minister Rimsky Yuen Kwok-keung, running in the legal subsector, and former health minister Sophia Chan Siu-chee, contesting in the medical and health services subsector. New faces from the finance sector include Citi Hong Kong CEO and head of banking Aveline San Pau-len and Standard Chartered Bank’s CEO for Hong Kong, Greater China and North Asia, Mary Huen Wai-yi.
Some major developers are seeking re-election, including Henderson Land Development chairman Martin Lee Ka-shing, Sino Land chairman Daryl Ng Win-kong, and CK Asset’s executive director Justin Chiu Kwok-hung.
Pacific Century Group chairman Richard Li Tzar-kai, younger son of Hong Kong’s richest tycoon Li Ka-shing, has signed up for the Employers’ Federation of Hong Kong subsector.
The election is also marked by the absence of opposition-leaning candidates. The only centrist Election Committee member, Tik Chi-yuen, who stepped down as a lawmaker last year, did not seek re-election in the social welfare sector.
Keener competition this year
This year’s Election Committee poll is markedly more competitive than the 2021 race, with 31 subsectors holding contested races, more than double the 13 five years ago.
Across the 31 subsectors, the social welfare and medical and health services subsectors face the fiercest battles, with 25 and 23 candidates respectively vying for the 15 seats in each.
All 18 subsectors under the industrial, commercial and financial sectors will hold contested elections, breaking with their long-standing practice of internal coordination to avoid competition. Among them, the commercial (second) and industrial (second) subsectors will stage contested polls for the first time.
Meanwhile, five subsectors are returned unopposed, including labour, education, associations of Chinese fellow townsmen, representatives of Hong Kong members of relevant national organisations, and sports, performing arts, culture and publication, accounting for 259 members.

Bernard Chan, chairman of Asia Financial Holdings and Asia Insurance and head of the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority board, casts his ballot at the Wan Chai polling station.
He says geopolitical tensions and technological advancements remain the greatest challenges for the next city leader and other public officeholders, placing them under intense pressure.
“I believe anyone taking up public office in the future will face major challenges they may never have encountered before,” Chan says.
He notes that the current government has helped Hong Kong get back on track after the chaos following the 2019 social unrest while tackling numerous difficulties.
“However, these challenges will keep coming; they are not short-term challenges, including geopolitics and new technologies that upend our economic model,” Chan adds.
“I hope that all elected Election Committee members can make the right choices regarding Hong Kong’s future development and that of the country.”
Voter turnout surpasses 2021 total
As of 1pm, turnout for the Election Committee poll stands at 89.81 per cent – already surpassing the 89.77 per cent overall turnout recorded in 2021.
So far, 5,127 of the 5,709 eligible electors have cast their ballots.
Across the 31 contested subsectors, commercial (third) and technology and innovation see a 100 per cent turnout, the highest among all subsectors.
Another 10 subsectors see turnout rates above 90 per cent, including commercial (first), wholesale and retail, and legal and grass roots associations.
Social welfare remains the subsector with the lowest turnout, standing at 60.74 per cent.
Vote count to be completed within ‘reasonable time frame’
While the 2021 poll took more than 14 hours to count votes because of glitches in the counting machines, Electoral Affairs Commission chairman David Lok Kai-hong says authorities reviewed the process after the previous election and improved the electronic counting systems, which ran smoothly and efficiently in last year’s by-election.
“The Electoral Affairs Commission generally does not predict how long vote counting will take. From our perspective, the most important thing is that the election is fair and impartial,” Lok says.
“But I think I can say here that we are confident the vote counting this time can be completed within a reasonable time frame.”
Electoral Affairs Commission chairman David Lok (second right) says vote counting can be completed “within a reasonable time frame”. Photo: Karma Lo
Lok is also satisfied with this morning’s voting procedures, saying polling stations are running smoothly and electors are casting their ballots in an orderly manner with sufficient voting booths, despite large numbers of voters flocking to the polls.
“The Electoral Affairs Commission does not comment on the turnout rate, nor do we set any target for voter turnout,” Lok adds.
“We certainly hope to encourage and appeal to all eligible voters to please come out and cast their ballots today.”
Speaking to the media after inspecting a polling station in Wan Chai, Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak Mei-kuen says the election atmosphere is enthusiastic and orderly.
“Every candidate and their campaign team wants to build recognition and win support from voters. Everyone can see that things have been very orderly,” Mak says.
“It reflects Hong Kong’s democratic development; everyone is making progress towards high-quality democracy.”
‘John Lee is very competent’
Chan Wing-kee, a former standing committee member of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference and a candidate in the industrial (second) subsector, praises city leader Lee’s performance.
“Let’s see how things develop. I am very satisfied with the incumbent chief executive,” Chan says.
“I think the current chief executive is very competent, and I am also quite satisfied with how he has handled various matters.”
However, he stops short of saying whether he will support Lee for a second term.
“Hong Kong has many capable people, so whoever becomes the next chief executive, I will vote for the one with the strongest ability,” Chan adds.
“If I become an Election Committee member, I will choose the most capable candidate, although that doesn’t mean their opponent isn’t good.”
When asked whether he expects a contest in the next city leader race, he says the situation remains unclear. “We’ll just see how things unfold,” he adds
Meanwhile, Wingco Lo Kam-wing, president of the Chinese Manufacturers’ Association of Hong Kong, says he expects elected members to lead the industrial sector’s upgrading and transformation.
As an ex officio member, he also calls on the next city leader to implement Hong Kong’s first five-year plan well.
“Hong Kong’s economy must transform. Alongside our traditional industries, we need to cultivate more emerging sectors while building [the city] into an international innovation and technology centre,” Lo says.
“That will take an all-of-society effort, with both the government and the business community working together to foster Hong Kong’s future economic development.”
More tycoons have also been seen casting their ballots at the polling station in Wan Chai, including Henry Cheng Kar-shun, chairman of New World Development, and Douglas Woo Chun-kuen, chairman of Wheelock and Company Limited.
Highly competitive race: Regina Ip
Regina Ip Lau Suk-yee, chairwoman of the New People’s Party, canvasses for her party’s candidates outside the polling station in Wan Chai. She describes the race as “highly competitive”, noting the vibrant atmosphere and long queues at the polling station.
“We are a small party. We have a limited number of candidates in the commerce subsectors, mostly in the district committees subsectors,” Ip says. “We are aiming for a 90 per cent success rate.”
She declines to comment on next year’s chief executive election.
Convenor of the Executive Council Regina Ip (second left) at the Harbour Road Sports Centre polling station in Wan Chai. Photo: Karma Lo
Meanwhile, Lo Wai-kwok, chairman of the Business and Professionals Alliance for Hong Kong, expresses confidence that elected Election Committee members will choose the next chief executive wisely, and calls on eligible electors to cast their ballots.
“Competition in this election is intense. Each subsector draws top talent across generations, including newcomers and veterans,” Lo says. “This merit-based selection process will produce Election Committee members we can truly rely on.”
However, Lo declines to comment on the next city leader, stressing only that the person should go all out to improve Hong Kong’s economy and people’s livelihoods.
“In our exchanges [with voters], we’ve had in-depth discussions on advancing Hong Kong’s economy and people’s livelihoods – especially the Northern Metropolis – and on how to align with national needs while playing to Hong Kong’s strengths,” he adds.
Turnout rate surpasses 80 per cent
A total of 4,740 voters have cast their ballots as of 12pm, representing an overall turnout of 83.03 per cent, significantly higher than the 45.92 per cent recorded during the same period in 2021.
Across the 31 contested subsectors, commercial (third), which represents the Hong Kong Chinese Enterprises Association, recorded a turnout of 100 per cent, the highest among all subsectors. All 113 voters of the subsector have voted.
The turnout of eight other subsectors has also surpassed 90 per cent, including commercial (first); industrial (first); legal; technology and innovation; agriculture and fisheries; grass roots associations; representatives of members of area committees, district fight crime committees and district fire safety committees of Hong Kong and Kowloon, and representatives of members of area committees, district fight crime committees and district fire safety committees of the New Territories.
The social welfare subsector has recorded the lowest turnout so far at 53.37 per cent.
Secretary for Constitutional and Mainland Affairs Janice Tse Siu-wa was seen inspecting the polling station in Wan Chai before noon.
‘Good atmosphere proves election’s value’
Lau Wing-keung, an elderly voter in the Heung Yee Kuk sector, visits the Kowloon Park Sports Centre polling station before 11am, noting that time slot is better to avoid the crowds.
He notes there are more people than the last election.
“It is much more convenient when they congregate the voting stations to a few places, that is less scattered,” Lau says.
“Canvassing for votes is a sort of support for the election. It has a good atmosphere, which proves the election is useful in electing the chief executive.”
Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak Mei-kuen visits the station in the morning and leaves at around 11.20am with her staff.
First hour sees record turnout of 45 per cent
Among the 5,709 registered voters, 2,554 cast their ballots in the first hour of polling, representing an overall turnout of 44.74 per cent, more than triple the 14.73 per cent recorded during the same period in 2021.
Across the 31 contested subsectors, commercial (third), which represents the Hong Kong Chinese Enterprises Association, records a turnout of 98.23 per cent, the highest among all subsectors.
The turnout in five other subsectors has also surpassed 50 per cent, including legal; industrial (first); agriculture and fisheries; grass roots associations; and representatives of members of area committees, district fight crime committees and district fire safety committees of Hong Kong and Kowloon.
By contrast, commercial (second), representing the Chinese General Chamber of Commerce, has recorded the lowest turnout so far at 16.16 per cent, with just 16 of its 99 registered voters having cast their ballots.
In the first hour of the 2021 election, the labour subsector recorded the highest turnout at 29.73 per cent, while education had the lowest at 7.49 per cent. Both subsectors are uncontested this year.
Kowloon Park Sports Centre polling station in Tsim Sha Tsui on Sunday. Photo: Karma Lo
Technology used for canvassing support, verification
Vincent Kwok, a technology sector voter in his early fifties, says he arrived at the Kowloon Park Sports Centre polling station at about 9.35am.
He notes that there is more enthusiastic canvassing by candidates and voters this time than last election.
“I feel the atmosphere is very good,” Kwok says. “Everyone wants to contribute to this.”
Despite waiting in line to vote, he says the arrangements are well organised.
“I had to wait in there. It seems it is more enthusiastic this year,” he says. “By my observation, I waited more than 10 minutes. There were around 70 to 80 people for my line.”
Kwok says voters were seated while waiting and the process was smooth.
“I thought we could go straight in but we had to sit,” Kwok says. “But it’s OK. It’s quite smooth.”
He says all candidates explained their platforms and directions to voters like him via WhatsApp, WeChat, email and online conference clearly.
He highlights the use of technology at the station, noting voters’ identities were double-checked and ballots were scanned for verification to ensure everyone voted successfully.
Over 100 voters line up before voting starts
Hundreds of campaigners canvass support by raising placards with candidates’ names, numbers and categories along Austin Road outside the polling station at Kowloon Park Sports Centre.
Voters gradually show up, walking to the station early Sunday morning.
Raymond Chui, 59, a voter for Representatives of members of Area Committees, District Fight Crime Committees, and District Fire Safety Committees of the New Territories, says he has come early to vote before going to work to support the election.
He says competition appears keener than the last election.
“I came around 8.45am. More than 100 people had already lined up there,” says Chui. “I was more than 150th in line.”
He notes that candidates are more enthusiastic in canvassing for support than last time.
“They were very enthusiastic, filling the road up to the taxi stop of B P International hotel,” Chui says.
Apart from taking to the streets, candidates tried to reach voters like him via WhatsApp, WeChat and physical mail, Chui adds.
Waiting times up to 30 minutes for voters in Wan Chai
As most voters head to the polls in the morning, some electors say they have been waiting nearly half an hour to cast their ballots at the Harbour Road Sports Centre polling station.
An insurance subsector voter, who asks to be identified only by his surname, Fung, says he sees more than 100 people queuing inside the venue and that it took him nearly 40 minutes to vote, though he stresses the overall process is smooth.
Lawmaker Jonathan Leung Chun, who is voting in the catering subsector, says he queued for 20 minutes, adding that instructions inside are clear despite the lengthy wait.
However, some electors have opted to leave and return later in the day because of the long lines. One voter who declines to give her name notes that more than 100 constituents were waiting and says she will come back later.
Voters wait in a seating area at Harbour Road Sport Centre polling station. Photo: Karma Lo
Outside the polling station, hundreds of campaign workers line both sides of the pedestrian walkways, chanting slogans and making final-stretch appeals for support.
Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung arrives at the polling station at around 9.15am to inspect security arrangements. More than a dozen police officers are deployed nearby, while Civil Aid Service personnel repeatedly urge campaign teams to keep the pathways clear for incoming voters.
Several prominent business figures have also turned up to vote, including Pacific Century Group chairman Richard Li Tzar-kai. He declines to speak to the media when asked about his expectations for the incoming Election Committee. Hopewell Holdings founder Gordon Wu Ying-sheung is also seen at the polling station.
Allan Zeman backs city leader Lee for another term
Voters have flocked to cast their ballots at the Harbour Road Sports Centre polling station.
Lan Kwai Fong Group chairman Allan Zeman, who is both a voter and a candidate seeking re-election in the catering subsector, voices support for Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu to run for a second term as the city’s leader.
“If he’s one of the candidates running, I will support [him for re-election],” Zeman says, praising Lee as an approachable leader with a results-oriented approach to governance.
“He has done a very good job. And speaking to other businesspeople, they all agree he’s one of the best we’ve had.”
Zeman also says he expects incoming Election Committee members to have a strong grasp of Hong Kong’s needs and help the city navigate geopolitical tensions.
Meanwhile, Tai Po district councillor Armstrong Lee Hon-cheung, a voter in the district representatives subsector, says he is weighing candidates based on their community service record.
“I mainly look at their past track record and commitment to district service, as well as whether they have substantive, concrete proposals for Hong Kong’s future,” Lee says.
“I hope to find someone with long-term vision and a sense of responsibility towards Hong Kong, who will genuinely carry out practical work on people’s livelihoods to help all sectors of society – especially the grass roots and the sandwich class.”
Polling stations open at 9am
Voters have filed into polling stations as they opened at 9am. The five voting stations are located in Harbour Road Sports Centre in Wan Chai, Kowloon Park Sports Centre in Tsim Sha Tsui, Tsuen Wan Sports Centre in Tsuen Wan, Tiu Keng Leng Sports Centre in Tseung Kwan O, and Che Kung Temple Sports Centre in Sha Tin.
Two dedicated polling stations have also been set up at Happy Valley Police Station and Shek Pik Prison for electors in custody.
The polling hours run from 9am to 6pm. After the poll closes, ballot papers will be transported to the counting station at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai for vote counting.
Harbour Road Sports Centre polling station. A total of 856 candidates are vying for 723 seats across the 31 subsectors. Photo: Karma Lo
Final push to boost voter turnout
In the run-up to the election, the government, political parties and community groups have stepped up mobilisation to urge electors to cast their ballots. Candidates have also ramped up street-level campaigning, with magnates and former senior officials taking to the streets to hand out leaflets.
Lau Siu-kai, a consultant to the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said Beijing hoped Election Committee members would bridge the gap with the general public through street-level campaigning and better represent their interests when selecting the city leader and lawmakers.
Tam Yiu-chung, a former Hong Kong member of the National People’s Congress Standing Committee, mainland China’s top legislative body, said earlier that the more competitive election would drive up voter turnout.
He anticipated the turnout rate would reach 90 per cent after more thorough mobilisation than the 2021 poll, a figure he described as one Beijing “will be pleased to see”.
Veteran political commentator Sonny Lo Shiu-hing also said that the turnout rate would signal the effectiveness of Beijing’s mobilisation in the final stretch, adding that higher voter participation would give the elected members greater legitimacy.
Heavyweights joining the race
Dozens of high-profile candidates, including former senior officials and tycoons, also stand in the race.
Prominent newcomers include former justice minister Rimsky Yuen Kwok-keung, running in the legal subsector, and former health minister Sophia Chan Siu-chee, contesting in the medical and health services subsector. New faces from the finance sector include Citi Hong Kong CEO and head of banking Aveline San Pau-len and Standard Chartered Bank’s CEO for Hong Kong, Greater China and North Asia, Mary Huen Wai-yi.
Some major developers are seeking re-election, including Henderson Land Development chairman Martin Lee Ka-shing, Sino Land chairman Daryl Ng Win-kong, and CK Asset’s executive director Justin Chiu Kwok-hung.
Pacific Century Group chairman Richard Li Tzar-kai, younger son of Hong Kong’s richest tycoon Li Ka-shing, has signed up for the Employers’ Federation of Hong Kong subsector.
The election is also marked by the absence of opposition-leaning candidates. The only centrist Election Committee member, Tik Chi-yuen, who stepped down as a lawmaker last year, did not seek re-election in the social welfare sector.
Keener competition this year
This year’s Election Committee poll is markedly more competitive than the 2021 race, with 31 subsectors holding contested races, more than double the 13 five years ago.
Across the 31 subsectors, the social welfare and medical and health services subsectors face the fiercest battles, with 25 and 23 candidates respectively vying for the 15 seats in each.
All 18 subsectors under the industrial, commercial and financial sectors will hold contested elections, breaking with their long-standing practice of internal coordination to avoid competition. Among them, the commercial (second) and industrial (second) subsectors will stage contested polls for the first time.
Meanwhile, five subsectors are returned unopposed, including labour, education, associations of Chinese fellow townsmen, representatives of Hong Kong members of relevant national organisations, and sports, performing arts, culture and publication, accounting for 259 members.

title_en: After tapping offshore trusts, China eyes a bigger fiscal prize: an estate tax
content_en:
China is already laying the groundwork to impose an inheritance tax, as officials look to shore up government finances and combat inequality.
China could impose a higher inheritance tax to shore up its government finances, analysts say. Photo: AFP
For the past few months, China has been raking in an extra 1.4 billion yuan (US$210 million) per day on average in tax revenue from a new levy targeting wealthy families’ offshore trusts.
The tax, introduced in July, has already netted 160 billion yuan (US$24 billion) so far. But it is still unlikely to be enough to relieve the pressure on China’s public finances, which have been hit hard by an economic slowdown and prolonged property downturn.
Now, as the dust settles on the offshore trust campaign, many in China are asking the same question: what will Beijing’s tax-raising drive target next?
That has led to speculation that China may finally make a change that could potentially represent a bigger shake-up of the country’s fiscal system: imposing an inheritance tax.
The move appears to fit with the tax drive’s goals. Beijing has made clear that it plans to focus on the ultra-wealthy and avoid placing extra burdens on ordinary working families.
The tax could also have a large impact, given that China is about to witness a vast transfer of wealth as the country’s first generation of entrepreneurs ages and prepares to pass on their fortunes to their heirs.
China’s inheritance-related tax regime is extremely generous by global standards. The mainland imposes a largely nominal stamp duty on inherited assets – at a current rate of 0.025 per cent.
By contrast, the United States’ top estate-tax rate is 40 per cent, while South Korea’s reaches as high as 60 per cent – a rate thrust into the spotlight recently by Samsung’s multibillion-dollar inheritance tax settlement.
Earlier this year, heirs of the late Samsung chairman Lee Kun-hee finished paying off a landmark 12 trillion won (US$9 billion) inheritance tax charge after a five-year repayment process, according to local media reports.
Beijing’s most recent official guidance on the matter came last October, when the Financial and Economic Affairs Committee of the National People’s Congress reviewed two delegates’ bills calling for an inheritance and gift tax.
It is critical to unlock new tax revenue streams without heaping extra tax burdens on ordinary workersLiu Yang, Dentons
The commission recognised the tax’s potential as a tool to mitigate inequality, yet noted a host of “unresolved challenges and problems” that warranted further study. It recommended that legislative proposals be put forward “in due course”.
“This amounts to a policy signal,” said Liu Yang, a lawyer at Beijing-based firm Dentons, in a post on the social app WeChat in August.
For Liu, the committee’s reply suggests that the question is no longer “whether” China will adopt an inheritance tax, but “when”. The lack of an inheritance tax is a clear hole in China’s push to promote “common prosperity”, she said.
“As the first cohort of wealth builders enters concentrated wealth handovers, the absence of such a tax leaves intergenerational wealth transfers largely outside the reach of redistributive safeguards,” Liu added.
Beijing is also now in a stronger position to impose the tax thanks to previous reforms, some analysts argue. One major practical obstacle – gathering data on household assets – is no longer a problem, according to Ye Yongqing, a tax partner Beijing-based law firm Anli Partners.
“China has put in place the technological foundation for an inheritance tax, thanks to the Golden Tax IV programme and direct alignment with the international Common Reporting Standard regime,” he said.
Piloted in 2021, Golden Tax IV moves beyond invoice-based tax controls to a digital-first framework. The system supports cross-agency surveillance, automatically matching contracts, invoices and capital flows by pooling data sets from banking systems, customs authorities, corporate registries and more.
Fiscal pressures, meanwhile, are pushing the central government to consider introducing an inheritance tax.
In the first quarter of the year, all 28 Chinese regions that released official data said their fiscal self-sufficiency ratios had fallen below 100 per cent – including prosperous municipalities Beijing and Shanghai.
“Against that backdrop, it is critical to unlock new tax revenue streams without heaping extra tax burdens on ordinary workers,” Liu said.
Based on China’s history of reforms and overseas examples, Liu predicted that the country’s top inheritance tax rate could reach 40 per cent, with targeted concessions available for families with multiple children.
“Past experience shows legislation for a new tax typically takes three to five years to be finalised,” she said. “That means an inheritance tax framework could emerge within the 15th five-year plan [spanning 2026 to 2030].”
But would Chinese businesses be able to withstand the blow if such a tax were rolled out? Analysts warn Beijing must tread carefully.
Ye said entrepreneurs craved policy predictability. “Fresh levies would cast a negative shadow over their future outlook.”
Goldman Sachs struck a similar tone in a research note published earlier this month, saying that stricter tax enforcement had “weakened” private sector confidence and market sentiment to some degree.
By Emma Ma
